newsitem.title: UK: UK denies Rifkind remarks show EMU policy shift.
newsitem.headline: UK denies Rifkind remarks show EMU policy shift.

text.p: British officials strenuously denied on Wednesday that remarks on economic and monetary union (EMU) by Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind signalled a change in government policy or threatened a split in the cabinet.
Rifkind, speaking earlier on BBC radio, said the government was not neutral on EMU. On balance, he said, it was hostile to the single currency planned for launch in 1999.

Questioned about Rifkind's comments, a senior official said he was expressing the position agreed by cabinet on January 23, when ministers argued for a delay in EMU on the grounds it was very unlikely the single currency could be launched safely.
Pressed to say whether Prime Minister John Major supported Rifkind's comments, the official said: "The prime minister agrees with the foreign secretary that policy was set out on January 23."

Major told parliament then that it was unlikely, though not impossible, that the single currency could proceed safely on January 1, 1999. If it did proceed without reliable convergence, Britain would not of course be part of it, he added.
"We've already said it would be dangerous to proceed and it was on that basis that the foreign secretary was speaking," the government official said.

Conservative Euro-sceptics opposed to closer European ties were jubilant at what they saw as a clear shift in position by Rifkind, but party chairman Brian Mawhinney said the foreign secretary was expressing government policy.

"He was speaking on behalf of the Cabinet. We have nothing to add," Mawhinney, accompanied by two other cabinet ministers, told reporters while campaigning in Wirral South, where a by-election will be held on February 27.
"It is very important that the country has a prime minister prepared to defend and extend Britain's national interests in Europe," Mawhinney added.
The reaction of Paddy Ashdown, leader of Britain's minority Liberal Democrats, was scathing.
"The government can't sustain a position on Europe for a week," he told reporters.
"The Conservatives... are becoming the edge of Europe' party and will become the out-of-Europe' party after the election. That is almost inevitable," Ashdown said.
